title: Do people care about which school they work for?
author: Nick Hart
summary: In the first of a series applying Buckingham and Goodall's Nine Lies About Work to schools, Nick Hart examines the lie that people care which school they work for. He accepts the authors' claim that a school's vision and values act as 'cultural plumage' that attracts recruits, while the day-to-day experience of an immediate team determines whether staff stay or leave. He notes that team experience varies more within schools than between them, and argues that broad vision statements are rarely specific enough to guide everyday situations, so leaders should clarify purpose in concrete, situational terms. Because teaching can be lonely, he urges leaders to map the formal and informal teams that exist, make their membership obvious and create time for them to collaborate. He endorses the authors' eight team-experience statements as a way for team leaders to know their people, but warns against generic leadership advice: such inquiry is superficial without deep knowledge of teaching and learning. He ends by arguing that senior leaders must recognise team leaders' role in setting climate and help them learn to lead.
points: Vision and values are 'cultural plumage' that attract recruits, but local team experience is what makes staff stay or leave.
Hart observes that team experience varies more within a school than between schools, so the headteacher's abstract vision matters less than the local team.
Leaders should map the formal and informal teams in their school, make membership explicit and protect time for them to collaborate, since teaching is often isolating.
Buckingham and Goodall's eight team-experience statements are useful, but only alongside deep knowledge of teaching and learning; generic leadership advice alone is superficial.
Leading a team is a learnable skill, so senior leaders should actively develop phase, subject, year and admin team leaders.
quotes: The authors claim that people may initially be drawn to an organisation but it’s their experience working in their immediate team that makes them want to stay or leave, not some sort of loyalty to the organisation.

Individual teachers’ practice and their professional satisfaction is influenced by the interactions in their local team far more than the sometimes abstract vision, values and best of intentions espoused by the Headteacher.
A counter argument is that they’ll rarely be specific enough to be truly useful for the huge variety of situations those working in schools encounter each day. Another is that they are all positive.
If local experience on one’s team is the reason that colleagues stay or leave, school leaders need to appreciate the different teams that exist and the roles that colleagues play in each one.
School leaders ought to make team constitution obvious and create time for them to interact, collaborate and solve problems.
The knowledge built from the authors’ prompts is hidden knowledge which is extremely valuable for leaders to know. But we must be careful of the allure of generic leadership advice.
Leading a team is not an innate talent; it can be learned and senior leaders ought to help team leaders to develop.
